# Leaflet

Portable, project-agnostic gotchas for the [Leaflet](https://leafletjs.com/) web-mapping library — loading it from a CDN, embedding a map in a page, and the marker/`divIcon` and plugin behaviours that bite regardless of which app renders the map. True for any Leaflet map read cold.

- **Load Leaflet — and every Leaflet plugin — from a version-pinned CDN URL with a Subresource-Integrity hash and `crossorigin`.** Pin the exact version (`leaflet@1.9.4`, not `@latest`) and carry `integrity="sha256-…"` + `crossorigin=""` on both the CSS `<link>` and the JS `<script>`, so an upgraded or tampered CDN asset can't silently change under the app. The trap is doing this for the core bundle but forgetting a plugin: pin and hash the plugin the same way, or the one un-pinned `<script>` is the hole. (Grounded in `index.html`, which pins+SRIs `leaflet@1.9.4` core yet loaded `leaflet.markercluster@1.5.3` without an `integrity` attribute — the inconsistency is the lesson.)

- **Feature-detect an optional Leaflet plugin before using it, and fall back to core when its CDN script didn't load.** A separate `<script>` for a plugin (markercluster, heat, draw, …) can silently fail to load while the base Leaflet bundle succeeds, leaving `L.markerClusterGroup` (etc.) undefined. Guard the call with `typeof L.markerClusterGroup === "function"` and, when it's absent, add markers straight to the map instead of throwing — the base map must still render. (Grounded in `js/app.js` `renderMarkers()`: the cluster group is created only behind the `typeof` guard, and each marker falls back to `marker.addTo(map)` when the plugin is unavailable.)

- **Default an embedded, mid-page map to `scrollWheelZoom: false` so it doesn't hijack the page scroll.** A map that isn't the whole viewport but grabs the wheel traps a reader who scrolls onto it. Construct it with `L.map(el, { scrollWheelZoom: false })` (or gate wheel-zoom behind a click/focus). (Grounded in `js/app.js` `initMap()`: `L.map("leaflet-map", { scrollWheelZoom: false })`.)

- **Keep the tile provider's attribution — it's a licence term, not decoration.** OpenStreetMap's tile-usage policy requires visible attribution, so the `attribution: '… © OpenStreetMap contributors'` on the `L.tileLayer(...)` must stay even when tidying the UI; stripping it breaks the licence. Set `maxZoom` to the provider's real ceiling (OSM tiles top out at 19) so Leaflet doesn't request zoom levels the provider doesn't serve. (Grounded in `js/app.js` `initMap()`: the OSM `tileLayer` carries the attribution string and `maxZoom: 19`.)

- **When a marker needs its own CSS `transform`, put it on an inner element, not the `divIcon` root — Leaflet writes an inline `transform` on the icon root to position it.** Leaflet positions every marker by writing an inline `transform: translate3d(...)` onto the icon's root element; a `transform` you set on that same root (to rotate or centre the glyph) is clobbered on the next reposition. Make the icon root a zero-size anchor (`iconSize: [0, 0]`, `iconAnchor: [0, 0]`) and apply your rotation/centring transform to a `<span>` inside its `html`, whose transform Leaflet never touches. (Grounded in `js/app.js`: the route arrowhead rotates an inner `.route-arrow` span, and the arrival-check pin uses a zero-size anchor root with the visible pill as an inner span, exactly to survive Leaflet's root transform.)

# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The nightly PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The fleet routine runs the
pack's one maintenance task (`repo-tidy`) against a repo; this is the policy it follows. The per-object
**method** lives in the pack's skills ([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

The `repo-tidy` pass applies each single-object skill across the targets the plan hands it, then
rewrites the repo's standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per repo, body rewritten
to today's state, a dated comment per run).

# AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model)

Portable, project-agnostic gotchas for the AWS Serverless Application Model and the API-Gateway/CloudFront stack it deploys — true for any SAM project read cold.

- **`BuildMethod: esbuild` strips the entry's subdirectory from the Handler path.** With a single entry point in a subdirectory (`EntryPoints: [src/handler.mjs]`), SAM's esbuild builder writes the bundle to `<artifact-root>/handler.js` — esbuild's default `outbase` is the entry's own dir. Set `Handler: handler.handler`, not `src/handler.handler`; `sam build` succeeds either way, and the wrong value fails only at first invoke with `Runtime.ImportModuleError: Cannot find module 'src/handler'`.
- **esbuild must be a regular `dependency`, not a `devDependency`.** SAM's esbuild builder runs a *production-only* `npm install` in its scratch dir, so a `devDependency` esbuild is skipped and the build fails with "Cannot find esbuild." Declare it in `dependencies`, or put it on the runner's `PATH` before `sam build`.
- **CloudFront won't forward `Authorization` via a *custom* origin-request policy** — a custom `AWS::CloudFront::OriginRequestPolicy` listing `Authorization` is rejected at deploy ("The parameter Headers contains Authorization that is not allowed"). To forward it to the origin while keeping it out of the cache key (so public GETs share one cached entry), attach the **managed** `AllViewerExceptHostHeader` policy (id `b689b0a8-53d0-40ab-baf2-68738e2966ac`) plus a custom cache policy that omits `Authorization`. Use the *ExceptHostHeader* variant specifically: forwarding the viewer `Host` to an API Gateway origin returns 403.
- **A deploy role must be able to drive the transform and CloudFront, or change-set creation fails with the real reason hidden.** The `Serverless-2016-10-31` transform runs as a macro, so the deploy principal needs `cloudformation:*`, and CloudFront management needs `cloudfront:*`, both at `Resource: "*"` (scope the *data-plane* grants to your stack instead). `sam deploy` surfaces only `Waiter ChangeSetCreateComplete failed` — the actual `AccessDenied` is visible only in the CloudFormation console's **Change sets** tab. Don't paper over it with `AdministratorAccess`.
- **A brand-new AWS account can't create a CloudFront distribution until AWS verifies it.** The deploy fails `AccessDenied: Your account must be verified before you can add new CloudFront resources` — an account-level anti-abuse gate, not an IAM or template bug. Open a Support case to get the account verified, and launch against the origin URL directly meanwhile.
- **A failed first `CREATE` must be cleaned up before you retry.** A stack left in `ROLLBACK_COMPLETE` (and a SAM managed-bucket stack stuck in `REVIEW_IN_PROGRESS`) can only be *deleted*, never updated. And any resource with `DeletionPolicy: Retain` survives the rollback orphaned, so the retry then fails `already exists` until you delete the orphan too.
- **API Gateway HTTP API (v2) rejects a `chrome-extension://` origin in CORS `AllowOrigins`** with `BadRequestException: Invalid format for origin`, accepting only `http(s)://…` or `*`. An API fronted by a browser-extension (or other non-`http`) origin must therefore set `AllowOrigins: ['*']` and rely on its **JWT authorizer**, not CORS, as the security boundary.
- **A CDN cache hit is served before the request reaches the origin or its authorizer**, so you cannot enforce request auth on a *cacheable* read without edge compute (Lambda@Edge) — and keying the cache per token destroys the hit rate that justified caching. Treat cacheable endpoints as public by design, and protect only uncached (write / per-user) paths at the authorizer.
- **Prefer a short CloudFront TTL over per-write cache invalidation.** Invalidation is billed per path beyond a small monthly free allowance, so a write-through design that invalidates on every write is a cost trap; a short TTL plus optimistic local rendering hides the propagation delay from the writer.
- **Bundle the AWS SDK into the Lambda artifact rather than relying on the managed runtime's copy.** The runtime doesn't ship every SDK sub-package (a missing one fails only at invoke), and its bundled SDK minor version drifts under you. Declare and bundle the SDK packages you import, and pin a non-EOL runtime explicitly rather than letting it float.
- **Review the change set before applying — `Replacement: True` on a stateful resource is a data-loss hard stop.** Replacement creates a *new, empty* resource; a DynamoDB table shows it whenever an immutable property (its `KeySchema`/`AttributeDefinitions`) changes. Enable stack **termination protection** too — it's a one-time CLI/API call (`update-termination-protection`), not expressible in the template body.
- **Adding a DynamoDB GSI does not backfill existing items.** The `UpdateTable` is additive and indexes only items that already carry the index's key attributes; rows written earlier stay invisible until each is rewritten with those attributes. Plan an explicit backfill pass if pre-existing data must appear in the new index.
- **A custom request header turns even a public GET into a preflighted CORS request.** Any non-simple header (e.g. a client-version header) makes the browser send an `OPTIONS` preflight, so the API's CORS `AllowHeaders` must list that header or the real request is blocked *in the browser* — while server-side unit tests that never run the CORS layer stay green.
- **Reach AWS from a session with the AWS CLI or a boto3 script — there is no AWS MCP tool.** A stack's real state comes from a CLI call (`aws cloudformation describe-stacks …`) — the last green deploy workflow only reports the last *deploy*, not the current stack state. The CLI is **not pre-installed on the cloud/web runner** (nor `boto3`/`sam`), so declare its install in the **environment setup script** (`pip install awscli`, or the official bundle) rather than per session; point it at the sandbox proxy's CA bundle (`AWS_CA_BUNDLE`) if a call fails TLS verification.

1	# Chrome extensions
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for building Chrome (and Chromium) extensions — manifest versions, background/service workers, content scripts, permissions, packaging and store review — true for any extension read cold.
4	
5	> **Releasing, versioning, and Chrome Web Store publication are standardized** — before building or changing any release/publish machinery in an extension repo, read the [chrome-extension-release standard](../chrome-extension-release/RELEASE.md) (its pack, declared when you're ready to ship) and copy its canonical workflows instead of re-deriving them.
6	
7	- An MV3 service worker's relative paths resolve against the worker's **own** file location, not the extension root. Any path handed to a Chrome API (`importScripts`, `action.setIcon`) or `fetch` must be extension-root absolute — a leading slash, or `chrome.runtime.getURL(...)`. A bare relative path silently fails: it can abort the worker on import, or make an API call reject with a fetch error while the worker keeps running.
8	- `declarativeContent` rules are evaluated by the **browser process**, not your extension — so a `SetIcon` action's image must already be raw pixels when the rule is registered; there is no later moment at which the extension gets asked to resolve one. A service worker has no DOM, so decode the packaged icon yourself: `fetch(getURL(icon)) → blob → createImageBitmap → OffscreenCanvas.drawImage → getImageData`.
9	- `chrome.events.UrlFilter`'s host operators are **raw string matches, not domain-boundary matches** — `hostSuffix: "example.com"` also matches `evilexample.com`, and `hostContains: "example"` matches any host containing that substring. `declarativeContent`'s `PageStateMatcher.pageUrl` gates an action icon or page condition on exactly these filters, so a **lookalike host silently satisfies a rule meant for your own site**. To mean *apex-or-any-subdomain*, combine `hostEquals: "example.com"` with `hostSuffix: ".example.com"` (the leading dot forces a label boundary); never gate a security- or origin-sensitive behavior on a bare `hostSuffix`.
10	- A shared global assembled by multiple injected content-script files, re-injected into the page on every activation (e.g. every popup open), must be **augmented**, never replaced — merge onto it (e.g. `Object.assign`), not `globalThis.X = {...}`, or each newly-injected file wipes what earlier files already attached. Likewise reset any state a file accumulates on each injection (e.g. a list a source pushes into) at load time, or it keeps growing across re-injections instead of staying per-load.
11	- Introspecting an MV3 service worker over CDP (`Runtime.evaluate` inside it) has two traps: `chrome.*` callback APIs don't reliably settle when awaited with `awaitPromise: true` (a hang with no internal timeout) — build the awaited signal from plain promises (`fetch`/`OffscreenCanvas`) instead of a `chrome.*` callback; and a bare top-level `function`/`const` isn't reachable from an injected evaluate — expose what the probe reads as an explicit `globalThis.x = …`. A dormant worker also has no globals until it re-runs its top level, and attaching to it is what starts that — so poll for the global rather than reading it once immediately after attaching.
12	- To authenticate an extension to a **JWT-validating** backend (an API Gateway JWT authorizer, any OIDC-validating server), obtain a Google **ID token** with `chrome.identity.launchWebAuthFlow` (`response_type=id_token`) against a Google Cloud OAuth client of type **Web application**, redirect to `https://<extension-id>.chromiumapp.org/` (from `chrome.identity.getRedirectURL()`), scope `openid email profile`, and **verify the returned `nonce`**. Do **not** use `chrome.identity.getAuthToken` — it returns an opaque OAuth *access* token (no verifiable signature/`iss`/`aud`) that a JWT authorizer rejects. Pin the extension id with a manifest `key` so the redirect URI stays fixed.

- `declarativeContent` rules are evaluated by the **browser process**, not your extension — so a `SetIcon` action's image must already be raw pixels when the rule is registered; there is no later moment at which the extension gets asked to resolve one. A service worker has no DOM, so decode the packaged icon yourself: `fetch(getURL(icon)) → blob → createImageBitmap → OffscreenCanvas.drawImage → getImageData`.
- `chrome.events.UrlFilter`'s host operators are **raw string matches, not domain-boundary matches** — `hostSuffix: "example.com"` also matches `evilexample.com`, and `hostContains: "example"` matches any host containing that substring. `declarativeContent`'s `PageStateMatcher.pageUrl` gates an action icon or page condition on exactly these filters, so a **lookalike host silently satisfies a rule meant for your own site**. To mean *apex-or-any-subdomain*, combine `hostEquals: "example.com"` with `hostSuffix: ".example.com"` (the leading dot forces a label boundary); never gate a security- or origin-sensitive behavior on a bare `hostSuffix`.
- A shared global assembled by multiple injected content-script files, re-injected into the page on every activation (e.g. every popup open), must be **augmented**, never replaced — merge onto it (e.g. `Object.assign`), not `globalThis.X = {...}`, or each newly-injected file wipes what earlier files already attached. # product-wiki — the self-growing product research wiki

This project keeps its market/user/competitor research as a self-growing wiki
under `product-wiki/` (Karpathy's LLM-wiki pattern: compile findings once, refine in
place). Layout, required page sections, growth-log dating, source links,
staleness, and the isolation wall are **check-enforced** — the finding is the
instruction, so this prose never restates them. The full growth procedure is
the pack's worker doc (`packs/product-wiki/run_daily/wiki-growth.worker.md`).

- **The sink is human-reviewed only.** `product-wiki/product-requirements/` never
  changes as a side effect of wiki work or any unattended pass — a wiki finding
  that should move a requirement gets a growth-log note (and a repo issue) and
  waits for a human. It is the only `product-wiki/` content the rest of the repo may
  build on.
- **Compile once, refine in place.** Read the target page end to end before
  researching; `## Open questions` is the backlog — research what it flags as
  open, thin, or dated, and spot-check an existing citation or two per pass.
  Never re-derive a claim that's already cited and current.
- **Cited, never silently rewritten.** An uncited claim doesn't get written. A
  wrong or superseded claim is corrected with a note of why (and its source),
  never deleted without trace. Every real change records itself in the page's
  growth log and updates the open questions in both directions.
- **No fabricated growth.** Most passes find little or nothing; no new citable
  material → no edit, no log entry, no PR. A padded update is worse than none.
- **sample-data and new wikis.** `product-wiki/sample-data/` gains a file only when
  a wiki claim needs one to point to — never test fixtures (anything a test
  asserts against belongs in engineering's tree). Any folder under `product-wiki/`
  outside the two reserved names *is* a wiki (the structural classifier), so
  create one only deliberately, seeded with its required sections; automation
  refines existing pages, it never invents new ones.
- **Review discipline.** Unattended growth always lands as an unmerged PR —
  researched claims entering a committed knowledge base need the review gate.
  The owner phrase **"grow the product wiki"** runs the worker method
  in-session with full web tooling: same rules, same PR discipline.

+- A **registered or static content script runs as a *classic* script — it can't be an ES module.** `chrome.scripting.registerContentScripts` and static `content_scripts` inject their files as classic scripts (there is no `type: 'module'` mode, unlike a page's `<script type="module">` or the module service worker), so a top-level `import` in one throws `Uncaught SyntaxError: Cannot use import statement outside a module` — **in the host page's console, not the extension's**. To load module code without a bundler, register a tiny **classic loader** whose only statement is a *dynamic* `import(chrome.runtime.getURL('…'))`: dynamic `import()` is legal in a classic script, and the module it pulls in runs in the same content-script isolated world with the content-script `chrome.*` surface intact. List that module **and its whole transitive import graph** under `web_accessible_resources` (gated to the target origins) or the fetch is blocked — and have a test walk the graph from the entry module so a newly-added import can't silently fall out of the list.
 - To put a menu on the **toolbar icon itself**, create it with `chrome.contextMenus.create({ contexts: ['action'], … })` — the `contextMenus` permission carries **no** install-time warning (unlike a broad host permission). Recreate the items with `contextMenus.removeAll()` first on install/startup so they self-heal instead of throwing on duplicate ids when the service worker re-runs its top level.

1	# Python
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
4	heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
5	most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
6	**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
7	optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
8	false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
9	itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
10	`python-optional-deps` skill.
11	
12	## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`
13	
14	The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
15	and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
16	`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
17	heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
18	(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`), so installing the package is cheap and the
19	heavy stack is pulled only when a user opts into the feature that needs it.
20	
21	The payoff is a test suite that runs anywhere with no ML/native toolchain: the offline
22	and mock paths exercise the whole pipeline, and CI never has to install TensorFlow or
23	Torch to be green. If a `pip install <pkg>` with no extra can't import the core, a heavy
24	dependency has leaked into the base set — move it to an extra. Whether a given dependency
25	is "heavy" enough to belong in an extra is a judgment about the package's shape, which is
26	why this stays prose.
27	
28	## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra
29	
30	Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
31	backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one. That
32	stdlib backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on, so the
33	full pipeline is exercised end-to-end without the ML or native stack ever being
34	installed. The heavy backend is then just one more implementation of the interface,
35	selected at runtime, never a hard import the core or the tests depend on. The clean
36	shape is a tiny backend interface plus a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the
37	*selected* backend by name — so the module that wires backends together never imports
38	any of them at load time, and adding a heavy backend never taxes the core.
39	
40	## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression
41	
42	An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
43	used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter
44	false-positive for unused-import (`F401`). Mark that line `# noqa: F401` and record the
45	deliberate suppression, rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.
46	Whether an import is a genuine probe or an accidental unused import is a judgment a
47	static scan can't make without a full unused-name analysis, so it stays prose.
48

# Python

Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
`python-optional-deps` skill.

## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`

The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`), so installing the package is cheap and the
heavy stack is pulled only when a user opts into the feature that needs it.

The payoff is a test suite that runs anywhere with no ML/native toolchain: the offline
and mock paths exercise the whole pipeline, and CI never has to install TensorFlow or
Torch to be green. If a `pip install <pkg>` with no extra can't import the core, a heavy
dependency has leaked into the base set — move it to an extra. Whether a given dependency
is "heavy" enough to belong in an extra is a judgment about the package's shape, which is
why this stays prose.

## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra

Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one. That
stdlib backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on, so the
full pipeline is exercised end-to-end without the ML or native stack ever being
installed. The heavy backend is then just one more implementation of the interface,
selected at runtime, never a hard import the core or the tests depend on. The clean
shape is a tiny backend interface plus a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the
*selected* backend by name — so the module that wires backends together never imports
any of them at load time, and adding a heavy backend never taxes the core.

## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression

An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter
false-positive for unused-import (`F401`). Mark that line `# noqa: F401` and record the
deliberate suppression, rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.
Whether an import is a genuine probe or an accidental unused import is a judgment a
static scan can't make without a full unused-name analysis, so it stays prose.

1	# sheepdog — the fleet enforcer marker
2	
3	Declaring this pack marks a repo as the **fleet enforcer**: the one repo that covers and maintains
4	every repo under an owner. It's opt-in — a dedicated `sheepdog` repo declares it (it is **not** seeded
5	by `--init`) — and it turns what used to be bespoke Claudinite fleet infrastructure into a declaration.
6	
7	The pack is thin. It contributes the one piece that only a fleet enforcer needs — the **census**
8	([check-fleet-coverage.mjs](check-fleet-coverage.mjs), the cross-repo walk) — plus its config schema
9	and the coverage-workflow stub. The rest of the machinery — running the daily-run (the orchestrator),
10	the run_daily engine, scheduling — is Claudinite **core** (`routines/`), because baselining and the
11	daily-run are Claudinite's own responsibility, not the pack's. Declaring `sheepdog` adds only the
12	cross-repo reach: the census, the owner/exclude config, and the token that spans the fleet.
13	
14	**Config** — this repo's `.claudinite-checks.json` carries, as its `packs` entry for this pack:
15	
16	```json
17	{ "id": "sheepdog", "config": { "owner": "missingbulb", "kind": "user", "exclude": ["owner/repo-a"] } }
18	```
19	
20	`owner` (default: this repo's owner) is who to cover; `exclude` is the repos deliberately kept out of
21	the fleet (a full `owner/name` each). `kind: "user"` today; org support is a later addition. This
22	replaces the old opt-out list — a repo is kept out by adding it here.
23	
24	**Classification** — the census is an ordinary **pack task**, not a fleet mechanism. Its
25	*implementation* — a workflow holding the account-spanning PAT — happens to scan every repo under the
26	owner, but its declaration, scheduling, and lifecycle are exactly those of any pack task: it is active
27	because this repo declares the pack, and it runs however this repo's tasks run. The cross-repo reach
28	lives in the implementation, never in how the task is wired. (The task file carries the same note.)
29	
30	**How it runs** — baselining materializes the [coverage workflow](stubs/fleet-coverage.yml) into this
31	repo and prompts for the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` secret (a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's repos:
32	Metadata + Contents read, Issues read/write, and Contents write on this repo for baseline-migration
33	retirement). That `workflow_dispatch`-only Action checks out Claudinite and runs this pack's census
34	([check-fleet-coverage.mjs](check-fleet-coverage.mjs)) with the token; it never
35	carries a `schedule:` of its own. This repo's single scheduled routine — the core orchestrator that
36	runs the daily-run ([routines/auto-all-repos-maintenance.md](../../routines/auto-all-repos-maintenance.md))
37	— is the one schedule ([routines/fleet/scheduling.md](../../routines/fleet/scheduling.md)).

Declaring this pack marks a repo as the **fleet enforcer**: the one repo that covers and maintains
every repo under an owner. It's opt-in — a dedicated `sheepdog` repo declares it (it is **not** seeded
by `--init`) — and it turns what used to be bespoke Claudinite fleet infrastructure into a declaration.

The pack is thin. It contributes the one piece that only a fleet enforcer needs — the **census**
([check-fleet-coverage.mjs](check-fleet-coverage.mjs), the cross-repo walk) — plus its config schema
and the coverage-workflow stub. The rest of the machinery — running the daily-run (the orchestrator),
the run_daily engine, scheduling — is Claudinite **core** (`routines/`), because baselining and the
daily-run are Claudinite's own responsibility, not the pack's. Declaring `sheepdog` adds only the
cross-repo reach: the census, the owner/exclude config, and the token that spans the fleet.

**Config** — this repo's `.claudinite-checks.json` carries, as its `packs` entry for this pack:

```json
{ "id": "sheepdog", "config": { "owner": "missingbulb", "kind": "user", "exclude": ["owner/repo-a"] } }
```

`owner` (default: this repo's owner) is who to cover; `exclude` is the repos deliberately kept out of
the fleet (a full `owner/name` each). `kind: "user"` today; org support is a later addition. This
replaces the old opt-out list — a repo is kept out by adding it here.

**Classification** — the census is an ordinary **pack task**, not a fleet mechanism. Its
*implementation* — a workflow holding the account-spanning PAT — happens to scan every repo under the
owner, but its declaration, scheduling, and lifecycle are exactly those of any pack task: it is active
because this repo declares the pack, and it runs however this repo's tasks run. The cross-repo reach
lives in the implementation, never in how the task is wired. (The task file carries the same note.)

**How it runs** — baselining materializes the [coverage workflow](stubs/fleet-coverage.yml) into this
repo and prompts for the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` secret (a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's repos:

([check-fleet-coverage.mjs](check-fleet-coverage.mjs)) with the token; it never

runs the daily-run ([routines/auto-all-repos-maintenance.md](../../routines/auto-all-repos-maintenance.md))
— is the one schedule ([routines/fleet/scheduling.md](../../routines/fleet/scheduling.md)).

1	# Firebase release — environments, provenance, attestation
2	
3	The release standard for Firebase-backed apps. **Decided ahead of first exercise** (from TLDR's
4	worked AWS split + the design in ShoutsAndWhispers `docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md`); refine on the first
5	real release rather than treating this as settled canon.
6	
7	## 1. The committed default is dev, always
8	
9	- **Two fully separate Firebase projects** — dev and prod. Isolation is at the project boundary
10	  (data, auth, quotas, keys), the Firebase analog of TLDR's separate AWS accounts.
11	- **Everything committed points at dev**: `.firebaserc`'s `default` alias, the checked-in client
12	  `firebase_options`, every documented command. Strongest form: **no prod alias committed at
13	  all** until the release milestone — no command run from the repo can reach prod by accident.
14	- **Dev builds coexist with prod installs** (Android `applicationIdSuffix .dev` / iOS bundle-id
15	  suffix) so testing on a real phone never displaces the store app.
16	- **Guard tests pin the contract** once prod exists: the committed client config's projectId must
17	  be the dev project (TLDR pins the equivalent in `client/test/inject-config.test.mjs`), and seed
18	  scripts hard-refuse prod targets.
19	
20	## 2. Prod config is release-pipeline-injected
21	
22	- The store artifact gets its prod `firebase_options` (and any prod-only identifiers) from
23	  **release-workflow variables**, never from the tree. A plain/local/CI build physically lacks
24	  prod coordinates.
25	- **The release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset** — a dev-pointed or
26	  placeholder-configured artifact must be unbuildable, not merely unlikely.
27	- The same artifact that goes to the store is the release download — one prod build, one
28	  provenance trail.
29	
30	## 3. Attestation beats provenance
31	
32	- Provenance (only the pipeline holds prod config) is necessary but not sufficient — anyone can
33	  extract config from a shipped APK/IPA. TLDR documents exactly this gap; Firebase can close it:
34	  **enforce App Check on the prod project** (Firestore, Functions, Storage) with Play Integrity
35	  (Android) / App Attest (iOS), so requests without a store-signed attestation are rejected
36	  server-side.
37	- **Dev keeps the App Check debug provider** so emulators, tests, and local builds stay
38	  friction-free; enforcement is a per-project switch, which is precisely why prod must be a
39	  separate project.
40	- Register the store apps in the Firebase console at first release; until enforcement is ON,
41	  treat prod as provenance-only and say so in the project's environments doc.
42	
43	## 4. Promotion is deliberate; dev deploys are automatic
44	
45	- Dev auto-deploys from `main` (it is the always-current sandbox); **prod deploys are a manual,
46	  explicit promotion** of something already verified in dev — a workflow dispatch or a named
47	  command, never a side effect.
48	- Per-environment deploy credentials: the prod deploy identity is distinct from dev's, so a
49	  compromised or misconfigured dev lane cannot touch prod.
50	- Data hygiene follows the project split: seed/backfill tooling targets dev by name and refuses
51	  the prod project id as a hard guard, not a convention.
52

# Firebase release — environments, provenance, attestation

The release standard for Firebase-backed apps. **Decided ahead of first exercise** (from TLDR's
worked AWS split + the design in ShoutsAndWhispers `docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md`); refine on the first
real release rather than treating this as settled canon.

## 1. The committed default is dev, always

- **Two fully separate Firebase projects** — dev and prod. Isolation is at the project boundary
  (data, auth, quotas, keys), the Firebase analog of TLDR's separate AWS accounts.
- **Everything committed points at dev**: `.firebaserc`'s `default` alias, the checked-in client
  `firebase_options`, every documented command. Strongest form: **no prod alias committed at
  all** until the release milestone — no command run from the repo can reach prod by accident.
- **Dev builds coexist with prod installs** (Android `applicationIdSuffix .dev` / iOS bundle-id
  suffix) so testing on a real phone never displaces the store app.
- **Guard tests pin the contract** once prod exists: the committed client config's projectId must
  be the dev project (TLDR pins the equivalent in `client/test/inject-config.test.mjs`), and seed
  scripts hard-refuse prod targets.

## 2. Prod config is release-pipeline-injected

- The store artifact gets its prod `firebase_options` (and any prod-only identifiers) from
  **release-workflow variables**, never from the tree. A plain/local/CI build physically lacks
  prod coordinates.
- **The release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset** — a dev-pointed or
  placeholder-configured artifact must be unbuildable, not merely unlikely.
- The same artifact that goes to the store is the release download — one prod build, one
  provenance trail.

## 3. Attestation beats provenance

- Provenance (only the pipeline holds prod config) is necessary but not sufficient — anyone can
  extract config from a shipped APK/IPA. TLDR documents exactly this gap; Firebase can close it:
  **enforce App Check on the prod project** (Firestore, Functions, Storage) with Play Integrity
  (Android) / App Attest (iOS), so requests without a store-signed attestation are rejected
  server-side.
- **Dev keeps the App Check debug provider** so emulators, tests, and local builds stay
  friction-free; enforcement is a per-project switch, which is precisely why prod must be a
  separate project.
- Register the store apps in the Firebase console at first release; until enforcement is ON,
  treat prod as provenance-only and say so in the project's environments doc.

## 4. Promotion is deliberate; dev deploys are automatic

- Dev auto-deploys from `main` (it is the always-current sandbox); **prod deploys are a manual,

# Python

Portable, project-agnostic practices for a Python package built around an optional
heavy/native dependency (an ML model, a native audio/GPU library, a cloud SDK) that
most of the codebase — and the whole test suite — must run without. The theme is one:
**keep the importable core dependency-free, and gate every heavy thing behind an
optional extra.** What stays here is the architecture judgment that has no
false-positive-free static signature; the mechanical shape of the optional import
itself (imported lazily, guarded with an install-hint re-raise) is carried by the
`python-optional-deps` skill.

## Keep the importable core dependency-free; heavy/native deps go in optional extras, not base `dependencies`

The core of a package (its logic, storage, CLI, any web/dashboard layer) should import
and run — and be **fully testable** — with only the Python standard library. Declare
`dependencies = []` (or the genuinely-always-needed minimum) in `[project]`, and put every
heavy, native, or ML dependency under a **named `[project.optional-dependencies]` extra**
(`pkg[yamnet]`, `pkg[speaker]`, `pkg[dev]`). The test: if a `pip install <pkg>` with no
extra can't import the core, a heavy dependency has leaked into the base set — move it
to an extra.

## Provide a stdlib-only implementation behind the same interface so tests and offline modes need no extra

Give the swappable interface a **dependency-free** implementation — a scripted/mock
backend built on the standard library alone — alongside the heavy real one; that stdlib
backend is what the test suite and any offline/`simulate` mode run on. The heavy backend
is then just one more implementation of the interface, selected at runtime, never a hard
import the core or the tests depend on. The clean shape is a tiny backend interface plus
a `load_default()`/registry that lazy-imports the *selected* backend by name, so the
module that wires backends together never imports any of them at load time.

## Mark the availability-probe import as a deliberate unused-import suppression

An import kept **only** to probe whether an optional stack is present (its name is never
used directly — the code just branches on whether the import succeeded) is a real linter
false-positive for unused-import (`F401`). Mark that line `# noqa: F401` and record the
deliberate suppression, rather than deleting the probe or letting the warning ride.

# sheepdog — the fleet enforcer marker

Declaring this pack marks a repo as the **fleet enforcer**: the one repo that covers and maintains
every repo under an owner. It's opt-in — a dedicated `sheepdog` repo declares it (it is **not** seeded
by `--init`).

It contributes the one piece that only a fleet enforcer needs — the **census**
([check-fleet-coverage.mjs](check-fleet-coverage.mjs), the cross-repo walk) — plus its config schema
and the coverage-workflow stub. The rest of the machinery — running the daily-run (the orchestrator),
the run_daily engine, scheduling — is Claudinite **core** (`routines/`), because baselining and the
daily-run are Claudinite's own responsibility, not the pack's.

**Config** — this repo's `.claudinite-checks.json` carries, as its `packs` entry for this pack:

```json
{ "id": "sheepdog", "config": { "owner": "missingbulb", "kind": "user", "exclude": ["owner/repo-a"] } }
```

`owner` (default: this repo's owner) is who to cover; `exclude` is the repos deliberately kept out of
the fleet (a full `owner/name` each) — a repo is kept out by adding it here. `kind: "user"` today; org
support is a later addition.

**Classification** — the census is an ordinary **pack task**, not a fleet mechanism. Its
*implementation* — a workflow holding the account-spanning PAT — happens to scan every repo under the
owner, but its declaration, scheduling, and lifecycle are exactly those of any pack task. The
cross-repo reach lives in the implementation, never in how the task is wired. (The task file carries
the same note.)

**How it runs** — baselining materializes the [coverage workflow](stubs/fleet-coverage.yml) into this
repo and prompts for the `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` secret (a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's repos:
Metadata + Contents read, Issues read/write, and Contents write on this repo for baseline-migration
retirement). That `workflow_dispatch`-only Action checks out Claudinite and runs this pack's census
([check-fleet-coverage.mjs](check-fleet-coverage.mjs)) with the token; it never
carries a `schedule:` of its own. This repo's single scheduled routine — the core orchestrator that
runs the daily-run ([routines/auto-all-repos-maintenance.md](../../routines/auto-all-repos-maintenance.md))
— is the one schedule ([routines/fleet/scheduling.md](../../routines/fleet/scheduling.md)).

# Firebase release — environments, provenance, attestation

The release standard for Firebase-backed apps. **Decided ahead of first exercise** (from TLDR's
worked AWS split + the design in ShoutsAndWhispers `docs/ENVIRONMENTS.md`); refine on the first
real release rather than treating this as settled canon.

## 1. The committed default is dev, always

- **Two fully separate Firebase projects** — dev and prod. Isolation is at the project boundary
  (data, auth, quotas, keys).
- **Everything committed points at dev**: `.firebaserc`'s `default` alias, the checked-in client
  `firebase_options`, every documented command. Strongest form: **no prod alias committed at
  all** until the release milestone — no command run from the repo can reach prod by accident.
- **Dev builds coexist with prod installs** (Android `applicationIdSuffix .dev` / iOS bundle-id
  suffix) so testing on a real phone never displaces the store app.
- **Guard tests pin the contract** once prod exists: the committed client config's projectId must
  be the dev project (TLDR pins the equivalent in `client/test/inject-config.test.mjs`), and seed
  scripts hard-refuse prod targets.

## 2. Prod config is release-pipeline-injected

- The store artifact gets its prod `firebase_options` (and any prod-only identifiers) from
  **release-workflow variables**, never from the tree. A plain/local/CI build physically lacks
  prod coordinates.
- **The release workflow fails if any injected variable is unset** — a dev-pointed or
  placeholder-configured artifact must be unbuildable, not merely unlikely.
- The same artifact that goes to the store is the release download — one prod build, one
  provenance trail.

## 3. Attestation beats provenance

- Provenance (only the pipeline holds prod config) is necessary but not sufficient — anyone can
  extract config from a shipped APK/IPA. Close the gap: **enforce App Check on the prod project**
  (Firestore, Functions, Storage) with Play Integrity (Android) / App Attest (iOS), so requests
  without a store-signed attestation are rejected server-side.
- **Dev keeps the App Check debug provider** so emulators, tests, and local builds stay
  friction-free; enforcement is a per-project switch, which is precisely why prod must be a
  separate project.
- Register the store apps in the Firebase console at first release; until enforcement is ON,

1	# Firebase
2	
3	Portable practices for repos built on Firebase (Auth, Firestore, Cloud Functions, FCM). Earned in
4	missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers; keep product-specific schema in the consuming repo's docs.
5	Environment separation (dev/prod projects, App Check, store gating) lives in the opt-in
6	[firebase-release](../firebase-release/RULES.md) pack — declare it when shipping gets close.
7	
8	## 1. Security rules are merge-aware and default-deny
9	
10	- **End every ruleset with an explicit catch-all deny** and grant per collection; a collection
11	  nobody thought about must be unreachable, not accidentally open.
12	- **Write rules against merge semantics, not just creates.** Clients using `set(merge: true)`
13	  surface the **post-merge** document in `request.resource.data` — a key-presence check that is
14	  right for `create` silently breaks on `update`. For updates, validate
15	  `request.resource.data.diff(resource.data).affectedKeys()` (what the client actually touched);
16	  for creates, validate `keys()`. This asymmetry is the single most common way a correct-looking
17	  ruleset rejects every legitimate client write.
18	- **Guard every field dereference for absence.** Distinct writers legitimately upsert disjoint
19	  field subsets of one doc; an unguarded `d.field` on a missing key throws and denies. Pattern:
20	  `!('field' in d) || <validation>`.
21	- **Server-owned fields are absent from the client-allowed key list**, not "checked for equality"
22	  — with `diff().affectedKeys().hasOnly([...])` a client physically cannot touch them (rate-limit
23	  stamps, server-computed aggregates).
24	- **Pin client timestamps to `request.time`** (`FieldValue.serverTimestamp()` satisfies it) on any
25	  write whose freshness matters — a client must not forge a heartbeat time — but scope the pin to
26	  writes that touch those fields, or unrelated single-field merges get rejected.
27	- **Bound every client-writable string/blob** (length caps in rules); an unbounded field is a
28	  free storage channel.
29	- **Admin-SDK code bypasses rules** — a rules review must enumerate what *functions* write too;
30	  "rules allow it" and "the system writes it" are different lists.
31	
32	## 2. Functions own identity, validation, and limits
33	
34	- **Identity comes from the verified token, never the request body** (`request.auth`,
35	  `token.name`/`picture` claims). Anything the client sends about *who they are* is decoration.
36	- **Validate inputs at the boundary like an adversary wrote them**: type-check, range-check
37	  (`NaN`/`Infinity` slip through naive numeric checks), length-cap, and enum-check before any
38	  read or write; reject with typed `HttpsError`s (`invalid-argument`, `unauthenticated`,
39	  `resource-exhausted`) so clients can react specifically.
40	- **Rate limits need a transaction.** A read-check-write cooldown is bypassable by firing calls
41	  concurrently; run the read + check + stamp inside `runTransaction` so concurrent invocations
42	  serialize. A thrown `HttpsError` inside the transaction aborts it and propagates unchanged.
43	- **Chunk batched writes well under the 500-op limit** and treat multi-batch fan-out as
44	  at-least-once: a mid-sequence crash plus client retry duplicates the early batches. Document
45	  the idempotency-key escape hatch even if v1 doesn't implement it.
46	- **Push is best-effort by construction**: notification failures must never fail the triggering
47	  call; clean up dead tokens on the *actual* error codes
48	  (`messaging/registration-token-not-registered` — verify codes against the installed
49	  firebase-admin, not memory or old blog posts).
50	
51	## 3. Test logic pure, rules empirically
52	
53	- **Extract decision logic into pure modules** (audience selection, filtering, formatting) so the
54	  default suite runs with zero emulators and zero mocks of the Firebase SDK.
55	- **When rules themselves are under test, test them empirically** with
56	  `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` against the real emulator — simulate each *exact client write
57	  shape* the app performs (create vs merge-update vs single-field token write) plus each
58	  forbidden shape. Reading rules and believing them is how the merge-semantics bugs above ship.
59	- **Cross-language contracts get mirrored test vectors.** When client and server must compute the
60	  same derived value (a geohash, a normalization), commit identical input→output vectors in both
61	  suites and diff the literals in CI — "both use the standard algorithm" is not a proof.
62	
63	## 4. Deploy layout and aliases
64	
65	- **Keep the Firebase project root self-contained** — the directory holding `firebase.json`, its
66	  `.firebaserc`, rules/indexes, and `functions/`. That root may be the repo root or a dedicated
67	  subfolder (e.g. `firebase/`); the CLI walks up to find `firebase.json` and resolves every path
68	  inside it *relative to that file*, so a subfolder needs no path edits — just run deploys from it
69	  (or pass `--config <dir>/firebase.json`). Keep compiled output (`functions/lib/`) and
70	  `.firebase/` gitignored.
71	- **Commit `.firebaserc` with named aliases and make the default the safe target** (see
72	  firebase-release for the full environment discipline). Deploy commands in docs always name
73	  what they deploy (`--only functions,firestore`) — an unqualified `firebase deploy` in a README
74	  eventually ships someone's half-finished hosting directory.
75	- **Smoke-load the built entrypoint in the test lane** (`node -e "require('./lib/index.js')"`).
76	  A Node-major skew between build and runtime, or a bad build, surfaces as a module crash the
77	  first time the deployed function is invoked — the cheapest place to see it is the suite.

Environment separation (dev/prod projects, App Check, store gating) lives in the opt-in
[firebase-release](../firebase-release/RULES.md) pack — declare it when shipping gets close.

## 1. Security rules are merge-aware and default-deny

- **End every ruleset with an explicit catch-all deny** and grant per collection; a collection
  nobody thought about must be unreachable, not accidentally open.
- **Write rules against merge semantics, not just creates.** Clients using `set(merge: true)`

  right for `create` silently breaks on `update`. For updates, validate
  `request.resource.data.diff(resource.data).affectedKeys()` (what the client actually touched);
  for creates, validate `keys()`. This asymmetry is the single most common way a correct-looking
  ruleset rejects every legitimate client write.
- **Guard every field dereference for absence.** Distinct writers legitimately upsert disjoint
  field subsets of one doc; an unguarded `d.field` on a missing key throws and denies. Pattern:
  `!('field' in d) || <validation>`.
- **Server-owned fields are absent from the client-allowed key list**, not "checked for equality"
  — with `diff().affectedKeys().hasOnly([...])` a client physically cannot touch them (rate-limit
  stamps, server-computed aggregates).
- **Pin client timestamps to `request.time`** (`FieldValue.serverTimestamp()` satisfies it) on any
  write whose freshness matters — a client must not forge a heartbeat time — but scope the pin to
  writes that touch those fields, or unrelated single-field merges get rejected.
- **Bound every client-writable string/blob** (length caps in rules); an unbounded field is a
  free storage channel.
- **Admin-SDK code bypasses rules** — a rules review must enumerate what *functions* write too;
  "rules allow it" and "the system writes it" are different lists.

## 2. Functions own identity, validation, and limits

- **Identity comes from the verified token, never the request body** (`request.auth`,
  `token.name`/`picture` claims). Anything the client sends about *who they are* is decoration.
- **Validate inputs at the boundary like an adversary wrote them**: type-check, range-check
  (`NaN`/`Infinity` slip through naive numeric checks), length-cap, and enum-check before any
  read or write; reject with typed `HttpsError`s (`invalid-argument`, `unauthenticated`,
  `resource-exhausted`) so clients can react specifically.
- **Rate limits need a transaction.** A read-check-write cooldown is bypassable by firing calls
  concurrently; run the read + check + stamp inside `runTransaction` so concurrent invocations
  serialize. A thrown `HttpsError` inside the transaction aborts it and propagates unchanged.
- **Chunk batched writes well under the 500-op limit** and treat multi-batch fan-out as
  at-least-once: a mid-sequence crash plus client retry duplicates the early batches. Document
  the idempotency-key escape hatch even if v1 doesn't implement it.
- **Push is best-effort by construction**: notification failures must never fail the triggering
  call; clean up dead tokens on the *actual* error codes
  (`messaging/registration-token-not-registered` — verify codes against the installed
  firebase-admin, not memory or old blog posts).

## 3. Test logic pure, rules empirically

- **Extract decision logic into pure modules** (audience selection, filtering, formatting) so the
  default suite runs with zero emulators and zero mocks of the Firebase SDK.
- **When rules themselves are under test, test them empirically** with
  `@firebase/rules-unit-testing` against the real emulator — simulate each *exact client write
  shape* the app performs (create vs merge-update vs single-field token write) plus each
  forbidden shape. Reading rules and believing them is how the merge-semantics bugs above ship.
- **Cross-language contracts get mirrored test vectors.** When client and server must compute the
  same derived value (a geohash, a normalization), commit identical input→output vectors in both

  subfolder (e.g. `firebase/`); the CLI walks up to find `firebase.json` and resolves every path

  (or pass `--config <dir>/firebase.json`). Keep compiled output (`functions/lib/`) and

- **Smoke-load the built entrypoint in the test lane** (`node -e "require('./lib/index.js')"`).

1	# Flutter
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for Flutter / Dart codebases — true for any Flutter project
4	read cold. Earned in missingbulb/ShoutsAndWhispers (a Firebase-backed, location-driven app with an
5	executable-requirements UI suite); keep anything project-specific in the consuming repo's docs.
6	
7	## Architecture: ports out of the widget tree
8	
9	- **Widgets depend on ports, never on plugins.** Every platform/backend concern (location, auth,
10	  push, backend calls, the clock) enters the UI as a hand-written abstract interface with pure-Dart
11	  value types; plugin adapters (`geolocator`, `firebase_*`, `google_sign_in`, …) implement them and
12	  are constructed **only** in `main.dart`. A plugin type leaking into a screen (a geolocator
13	  `Position`, a `FirebaseFunctionsException`) is a defect: it silently couples every widget test to
14	  the plugin's platform channels.
15	- **Enforce the boundary with a committed import-scan test** (dart:io over `lib/ui/`, `lib/screens/`
16	  looking for forbidden import prefixes). The analyzer won't stop a convenient leak; a five-line
17	  test does.
18	- **Ship the fakes in the package** (`lib/testing/`): scripted fakes for each port that also
19	  *record* what the UI asked of them, plus a `FakeWorld` bundling them with a pinned clock and the
20	  real app shell. Both the app's own tests and any sibling test package (e.g. an
21	  executable-requirements suite) import one fake world — never two parallel ones.
22	- **Extract the root shell into a widget** (`lib/app.dart`) taking the ports as parameters, used
23	  identically by `main.dart` (adapters) and the test harness (fakes). Tests must never rebuild a
24	  parallel MaterialApp — actuals come from the shipped shell.
25	- **Inject the clock.** Any widget that formats or compares times takes a `Clock` port; relative
26	  time rendered from `DateTime.now()` is untestable and drifts goldens.
27	
28	## Widget tests and goldens
29	
30	- **Load real fonts before any golden** — the test binding defaults to the glyph-less Ahem stub
31	  (text renders as boxes). Parse `FontManifest.json` from the root bundle and `FontLoader` every
32	  family (strip the `packages/<pkg>/` prefix so plain family names resolve), which also loads
33	  MaterialIcons; bundle text faces (e.g. Roboto) in the test package's pubspec. Watch for styles
34	  that don't inherit the theme's family — `ButtonStyle`/`styleFrom` text styles are the classic
35	  leak; pin `fontFamily` there explicitly.
36	- **Never `pumpAndSettle` around indeterminate progress indicators** — they schedule frames
37	  forever and the call never returns. Use fixed-duration pumps (`pump()` then
38	  `pump(Duration(...))`); this also makes an in-flight state (a spinner mid-send) a deterministic,
39	  golden-capturable frame. Corollary: after `tap()`, pump **twice** — one frame applies state, the
40	  fixed-duration pump advances implicit animations (ink ripples, color lerps) past the capture.
41	- **Anything that fetches must be injectable**: map tile providers, avatar images. Widget tests
42	  block real HTTP (a 400-returning stub client), so a `NetworkImage`/network `TileProvider` in the
43	  tree means error boxes, not screenshots. Provide a deterministic in-memory substitute (a
44	  canvas-drawn `ImageProvider` works and needs no asset files).
45	- **Fix the viewport per suite**: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `devicePixelRatio` to one
46	  phone-shaped size (and reset in teardown) so layout — and therefore goldens — can't drift with
47	  the harness default.
48	- **Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter.** A `start()` that awaits (permission check,
49	  first fix) can re-arm streams/timers after `stop()`/dispose ran mid-await; bump an epoch in
50	  `stop()` and bail after every await if it changed. The symptom (leaked GPS subscription after
51	  sign-out) is invisible in tests that don't await realistically.
52	
53	## Toolchain habits
54	
55	- **Verify plugin APIs against the installed source, not memory.** Major Flutter plugins break
56	  their APIs often (google_sign_in v7's `authenticate()`, flutter_map v7+'s options, geolocator's
57	  settings objects); resolved versions live in the pub cache
58	  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.
59	- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
60	  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
61	  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.
62	- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
63	  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
64	  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
65	  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.
66	- **The web sandbox ships no Flutter SDK.** Claude Code on the web boots without Flutter, so tests,
67	  `flutter analyze`, and golden regen can't run until it's installed. Install belongs in the
68	  environment **image** (built once, snapshotted, reused) — never a per-session hook that reinstalls
69	  every start. This pack declares that need in its `env` block ([pack.mjs](pack.mjs)); a project pastes
70	  one generic `environment-setup-command.sh` that runs every active pack's requirement via
71	  [engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs](../../engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs) and asserts it at session start (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md)
72	  Part 9).

  MaterialIcons; bundle text faces (e.g. Roboto) in the test package's pubspec. Watch for styles
  that don't inherit the theme's family — `ButtonStyle`/`styleFrom` text styles are the classic
  leak; pin `fontFamily` there explicitly.
- **Never `pumpAndSettle` around indeterminate progress indicators** — they schedule frames
  forever and the call never returns. Use fixed-duration pumps (`pump()` then
  `pump(Duration(...))`); this also makes an in-flight state (a spinner mid-send) a deterministic,
  golden-capturable frame. Corollary: after `tap()`, pump **twice** — one frame applies state, the
  fixed-duration pump advances implicit animations (ink ripples, color lerps) past the capture.
- **Anything that fetches must be injectable**: map tile providers, avatar images. Widget tests
  block real HTTP (a 400-returning stub client), so a `NetworkImage`/network `TileProvider` in the
  tree means error boxes, not screenshots. Provide a deterministic in-memory substitute (a
  canvas-drawn `ImageProvider` works and needs no asset files).
- **Fix the viewport per suite**: set `tester.view.physicalSize` and `devicePixelRatio` to one
  phone-shaped size (and reset in teardown) so layout — and therefore goldens — can't drift with
  the harness default.
- **Async lifecycle guards need an epoch counter.** A `start()` that awaits (permission check,
  first fix) can re-arm streams/timers after `stop()`/dispose ran mid-await; bump an epoch in
  `stop()` and bail after every await if it changed. The symptom (leaked GPS subscription after
  sign-out) is invisible in tests that don't await realistically.

## Toolchain habits

- **Verify plugin APIs against the installed source, not memory.** Major Flutter plugins break
  their APIs often (google_sign_in v7's `authenticate()`, flutter_map v7+'s options, geolocator's
  settings objects); resolved versions live in the pub cache
  (`~/.pub-cache/hosted/pub.dev/<pkg>-<ver>/lib/`) — read them before writing against them.
- **`flutter analyze` at zero issues** (infos included) is the bar a suite holds; lints that fight
  a deliberate convention (e.g. `file_names` vs. leaf-id case filenames) get disabled narrowly in
  that package's `analysis_options.yaml` with the reason as a comment.
- **Sandboxed/CI runners**: `flutter test` can stall for minutes at teardown on GPU-less containers
  with dropped sockets. The pattern that holds: stream output, kill the process group the moment
  the definitive marker prints (`All tests passed!` / `Some tests failed`), watchdog-kill on output
  silence. On healthy machines plain `flutter test` is equivalent — keep the wrapper thin.
- **The web sandbox ships no Flutter SDK.** Claude Code on the web boots without Flutter, so tests,
  `flutter analyze`, and golden regen can't run until it's installed. Install belongs in the
  environment **image** (built once, snapshotted, reused) — never a per-session hook that reinstalls
  every start. This pack declares that need in its `env` block ([pack.mjs](pack.mjs)); a project pastes
  one generic `environment-setup-command.sh` that runs every active pack's requirement via
  [engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs](../../engine/pack_loader/env-requirements.mjs) and asserts it at session start (see [bootstrap.md](../../bootstrap.md)
  Part 9).

1	# Web Speech APIs
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for browser voice I/O — speech-to-text
4	(`webkitSpeechRecognition` / the Web Speech `SpeechRecognition` API) and
5	text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`) — true for any app that reads
6	or listens through the browser, read cold. These are runtime browser-behaviour
7	gotchas, knowledge you carry into the code rather than state a tool can read off
8	the repo.
9	
10	> Some of these APIs (`chrome.tts`) are extension-only; where a rule touches
11	> MV3 service-worker / content-script mechanics, the general extension gotchas
12	> live in the [`chrome-extension`](../chrome-extension/RULES.md) pack.
13	
14	## Speech-to-text (`webkitSpeechRecognition` / Web Speech API)
15	
16	- **The recognizer owns its own microphone capture — you cannot hand it
17	  `getUserMedia` audio constraints.** `echoCancellation` / `noiseSuppression` /
18	  `autoGainControl` are `getUserMedia` *microphone* constraints, and the recognizer
19	  exposes no hook to set them on its internal stream (Chrome applies its default
20	  echo cancellation there regardless). To *warm* the device with a known processing
21	  state — and to read back whether echo cancellation actually engaged — run a
22	  separate preflight `getUserMedia({ audio: {…} })` capture and stop its tracks; the
23	  recognizer still captures on its own. (`suppressLocalAudioPlayback` /
24	  `restrictOwnAudio` are `getDisplayMedia` *screen-capture* constraints and have no
25	  bearing on a mic — don't reach for them here.)
26	- **Read the whole n-best list, not just alternative `[0]`.** Set
27	  `maxAlternatives` > 1 and iterate `result[0..length]` for `{ transcript,
28	  confidence }`; the ranked alternatives are exactly where homophone / near-miss
29	  recovery lives, and taking only the top hypothesis throws that away.
30	- **`onresult`, `onend`, and `onerror` all fire — settle the cycle exactly once.**
31	  Guard a `settled` flag: interim results arrive before the final one, a cycle can
32	  end with no result at all (treat `onend`-without-result as `no-speech`), and an
33	  error and an end can both arrive. The first terminal signal wins; later ones are
34	  ignored.
35	- **With `interimResults` off, engines omit `isFinal` — treat a result as final
36	  unless `isFinal === false`.** Don't test `if (result.isFinal)` (it's `undefined`
37	  on those engines and you'll drop every result); test `result.isFinal !== false`.
38	- **The classic recognizer streams audio to a cloud service (Google's) — plan for
39	  it.** A `network` error means "offline / service unreachable", and audio leaves
40	  the machine. On-device recognition is opt-in and capability-gated: probe
41	  `SpeechRecognition.available({ langs, processLocally: true }) === 'available'`
42	  once and cache it, set `recognizer.processLocally = true`, and **never trigger a
43	  language-pack download** (only `'available'` counts, not `'downloadable'`). When
44	  the local path is absent, fall back to ordinary cloud recognition unchanged.
45	- **Contextual biasing (`SpeechRecognitionPhrase` + `recognizer.phrases`) works
46	  only on the on-device path** — gate it behind that same availability probe and
47	  apply it best-effort (any failure falls back to un-biased recognition rather than
48	  breaking the listen cycle). Only bias **closed vocabularies you control**
49	  (a command lexicon, known labels, a spelling alphabet) with **modest** boosts:
50	  over-boosting makes the recognizer hear a biased phrase when the user actually
51	  said a same-sounding free-form utterance.
52	- **Map the raw Web Speech error names to a small taxonomy** — `not-allowed` /
53	  `service-not-allowed` → permission-denied, plus `no-speech`, `network`,
54	  `aborted`, `audio-capture`, else `other`. In particular `aborted` is the
55	  *self-inflicted* stop (you called `recognizer.abort()`), so the caller should
56	  ignore it rather than surface it as a failure.
57	- **A missed endpoint mid-utterance needs a pause watchdog, not just `onend`.**
58	  If interim hypotheses exist but no final arrives, the engine may have lost the
59	  endpoint; a timer that fires after a pause discards the half-heard input and
60	  reopens a fresh cycle (preventing "heart heart" doubles when the user repeats
61	  themselves). Set the threshold **well above a natural mid-command thinking
62	  pause** — a tight window (~1.2 s) cuts real commands; a wider one (~1.8 s) keeps
63	  only the genuine missed-endpoint case.
64	- **Mic permission is per-origin, and the grant belongs to whatever page the
65	  recognizer runs in.** In a content script the prompt reads as the *host site*
66	  asking and the grant persists for that origin. Surface it in a controlled moment:
67	  preflight `navigator.permissions.query({ name: 'microphone' })`, then a one-time
68	  `getUserMedia` to raise the prompt. **Retry the capture bare** (`{ audio: true }`)
69	  if the first constrained call is rejected — a browser balking at the constraint
70	  *shape* must not be misread as a permission denial; only a second failure is a
71	  real "denied".
72	
73	## Text-to-speech (`chrome.tts` / `speechSynthesis`)
74	
75	- **Prefer `chrome.tts` over `speechSynthesis` — it's immune to page
76	  autoplay / user-activation gating.** `speechSynthesis` invoked from a content
77	  script is subject to the host page's autoplay policy and can silently refuse to
78	  speak; `chrome.tts` (extension-only, needs the `"tts"` permission, usable from the
79	  service worker) is not. Make `chrome.tts` primary and `speechSynthesis` the
80	  fallback for non-extension document contexts.
81	- **`chrome.tts` doesn't exist in a content script — relay speak/cancel to the
82	  service worker over a port.** Keep the same `speak()`/`cancel()` contract on both
83	  sides; the in-page port sends `{ speak }` / `{ cancel }` messages and the worker
84	  drives `chrome.tts`. On port disconnect, resolve every pending `speak()` promise
85	  so a dead worker never leaves the caller awaiting an utterance that will never
86	  finish.
87	- **Voice lists load lazily — an empty `getVoices()` means "not ready yet", not
88	  "no voices".** Resolve the preferred voice on the *first* `speak()` and don't
89	  cache an empty result: fall back to the default that turn and try to resolve
90	  again next turn.
91	- **Don't trust the OS/browser default voice — it's often the most robotic one
92	  installed.** Keep an ordered list of preferred voice names, take the first one
93	  actually installed, and fall back to the default only when none match.
94	- **Resolve a `speak()` promise on *any* terminal event, and never reject.** For
95	  `chrome.tts` that's `end` / `interrupted` / `cancelled` / `error`; for
96	  `speechSynthesis` it's `onend` / `onerror`. Resolving (not rejecting) on error
97	  keeps a spoken-prompt sequence from deadlocking on one bad utterance. Use
98	  `enqueue: false` so a new line interrupts the current one for turn-taking rather
99	  than stacking up.
100	- **Neither engine reliably supports SSML — you can't force intonation.** If a
101	  punctuation cue matters (a question's rising tone), speak the cue in words
102	  ("question mark") rather than relying on prosody the engine may not apply.

1	# Executable requirements — the framework standard
2	
3	The concrete conventions for running a numbered spec as tests. The judgment layer — doc-first
4	red-by-default, owner-owned expecteds, honest-gap tracking — is the
5	[spec-driven-product](../spec-driven-product/RULES.md) playbook; this pack is the mechanics that
6	implement it, so a new project or a new stack adopts the framework by convention instead of
7	re-deriving it. Worked implementations: GoogleCalendarEventCreator (origin; extension/jsdom
8	rendering), TLDR (adds a cross-tier `server` kind), ShoutsAndWhispers (Flutter port; first `saga`
9	kind).
10	
11	## 1. The layout is the contract
12	
13	- Everything lives under **`dev/requirements/`**: `requirements.md` (the numbered prose spec),
14	  one **top-level folder per kind**, `shared/` for cross-kind infra, and the runners/gates. The
15	  spec file's path is the framework's structural fingerprint — this pack activates on it.
16	- **A requirement line** starts (optionally after a list dash) with a backtick-wrapped dotted
17	  number: `` `4.2` ``. A **leaf** is an id with no finer-numbered child. Parse with one shared
18	  regex (`` ^\s*(?:-\s+)?`(\d+(?:\.\d+)+)` ``) so specs stay drop-in compatible across projects.
19	- **The folder is the kind.** A case's kind is the directory it lives in — the case declares no
20	  kind field, so classification cannot drift. Cases are
21	  `<kind>/cases/<slug>.<leaf-id>.case.<ext>`: a stable feature slug (so retitling a spec section
22	  never forces renames), then the dotted leaf id. The filename **is** the leaf link.
23	- **Artifact expecteds live beside their case** (`<slug>.<id>.png`, `expected/<name>.json`);
24	  failure artifacts (actual/diff renders) go to a gitignored dir, never beside the goldens.
25	- Where the language discovers cases dynamically (Node `require`), the registry walks the
26	  folders; where it cannot (Dart/Flutter), each kind keeps a hand-written `manifest` and **the
27	  gate enforces manifest ⇄ disk equality** — a case file that exists but isn't registered never
28	  runs, so unregistered must be red.
29	
30	## 2. What the coverage gate checks
31	
32	The bijection gate is one committed test, and it is the framework's spine. It must fail on every
33	one of: a leaf no case claims (doc-first red-by-default); a case claiming a non-existent leaf; two
34	cases claiming one leaf; a misnamed case file; a kind directory absent from the registry (or a
35	registered kind with no directory); a manifest out of sync with disk (where manifests exist); an
36	image found in a coded kind's folder (a screenshot cannot verify a gesture or a pure rule); a
37	stray golden no case or step accounts for. Every rule iterates the registry — adding a kind never
38	edits the gate.
39	
40	The gate checks repo state; an interactive feature run also has an *ordering*: after the
41	owner's feature-classified comment, an independent commit updating the spec (no code alongside)
42	precedes the first code commit on the branch. The spec's path defaults to the canonical
43	`dev/requirements/requirements.md`; a project whose spec lives elsewhere (a non-canonical
44	layout, or the pack pulled in via a `requires` from `spec-driven-product`) names it on the pack
45	entry as `config.spec`.
46	
47	## 3. The kind vocabulary
48	
49	Recurring kinds, by what they can honestly observe — route each leaf to the kind that can actually

51
